extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, potential authors and editors interested in arXiv-overlay/open-access journal policies
extracted.subtask_description: Policies, scope, and quality standards for running/publishing in an arXiv-overlay mathematics journal (Discrete Analysis). Covers submission/fee policy, editorial practices, website/usability expectations, versioning, and acceptance heuristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope: reasonably broad but not foreign to editors
rubrics_metrics.description: We want to be reasonably broad. If a paper is good enough, then we will not be too worried about whether it has the right sort of subject matter, as long as it isn’t in an area that is completely foreign to the editorial board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the analysis in a paper by Hytönen, Li and Naor was accepted despite not being 'discrete' because it had a similar spirit (treating discrete structures with analytic tools). The rule is pragmatic: good-enough work with affinity to the board's expertise is within scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality: set a high bar and reject respectable papers if necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: We have been surprised and gratified by the high standard of submissions which has allowed us to set a high bar, turn away some perfectly respectable papers, and establish Discrete Analysis as a distinctly good journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to demonstrate that low-cost publishing is compatible with high mathematical and editorial quality; be prepared to reject papers even if respectable to maintain standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance heuristic based on editorial-introduction imaginability
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule of thumb: an article is acceptable in my judgment if and only if I can imagine an editorial introduction that would be accurate and that would convince a reasonable number of readers to check out the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial introductions are used as a proxy for assessing an article's story/interest; this heuristic replaces simple reliance on 'which journal' to judge quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: No artificial page/issue limits; continuous publication
rubrics_metrics.description: We are not artificially constrained by the need to fill a certain number of pages per year. We just have a standard we are aiming for and will accept all articles that we judge to reach it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish articles as soon as ready; there are no 'issues' or quotas—acceptance is driven solely by meeting the standard, not by space considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journals' primary role: organizing peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: In the internet age the only important function left for journals is organizing peer review. Since this is done through voluntary academic work, it should in principle be possible to run a journal for almost nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The overlay model emphasizes organizing refereeing and curation while using arXiv for dissemination; minimize other rent-seeking functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial introductions: provide context and actionable information
rubrics_metrics.description: Each article gives an option 'Editorial introduction' which sets the article in context and helps readers judge whether they might want to read it on the arXiv.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introductions can be written using information from the article itself, prior knowledge, referees' remarks, editors' remarks, and internet findings. They are displayed inline (not on a new page) to facilitate browsing and to share useful information usually hidden by private referee reports, without divulging private remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Version-of-record and arXiv-updates policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The accepted version becomes the version of record; however, because articles live on arXiv authors can update their arXiv preprint later and the arXiv page will indicate that the version is not the latest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submission workflow: after acceptance, authors submit a revision to arXiv incorporating referees' comments; the journal ensures editorial introduction and metadata are in place and 'publishes' by linking to the arXiv version. Readers get both a fixed record and visibility of later updates via arXiv.

rubrics_metrics.name: Website usability and design standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal's website should be attractive to look at, allow exploration of content without undue clicking/loading, handle basic LaTeX, show an image associated with each article, and work well on phones as well as laptops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design choices (e.g., images for articles) can make browsing easier and more engaging; aim for a browsing experience reminiscent of print journals while leveraging electronic affordances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission fee and author-charge policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholastica charges $10 per submission. Discrete Analysis does not pass this charge on to authors; a small fund covers it. Total costs per accepted article are about $15–$30 when accounting for acceptance rates and DOIs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep submission/processing costs minimal and, where possible, avoid charging authors. Compare favourably with high article processing charges from legacy publishers.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOI and metadata policy (CrossRef membership)
rubrics_metrics.description: The journal takes a subscription to CrossRef to enable issuing DOIs to articles; bibliographic entries use the format 'Title, Discrete Analysis year:number' where the number is the article number in that year, not a volume/issue number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May add number of pages to bibliographic entries (e.g., 'Discrete Analysis 2016:5, 43 pp.'). DOIs are used to help the journal 'play along' with existing systems (impact factors, metadata), even if one is critical of those systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bibliographic/identifier conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Article numbering uses year:number (article number within the year) rather than volume/issue; provide guidance on how to form BibTeX entries and whether to include page counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about citation format so authors know how to cite a Discrete Analysis article; consider optional tweaks to make BibTeX output easier.

rubrics_metrics.name: LaTeX/style-file policy and accepted-version footnote
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no preferred LaTeX class style for submissions to keep submission simple; an optional style file could be offered and the journal might require a footnote in the accepted version indicating it has been published in Discrete Analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplicity for authors is prioritized; optional uniform styling for the version of record can be considered but is not mandatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Featured-article selection practice
rubrics_metrics.description: At any one time the journal has a 'featured article'. Selection policy is undecided; for the launch the featured paper was both notable (solved a notable problem) and happened to be the first accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial board to decide democratically; one inclination is that each article should be featured at some point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling of rejected papers and reuse of referee reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Author resubmission practices: when a paper is rejected with a detailed referee report that deems the paper correct, authors could resubmit elsewhere together with a note that editors of the first journal might be consulted to save reviewing labour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The editor is broadly in favour of labor-saving transfer practices but cautions about hostile referees who might block other venues; no formal implementation specified yet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility and ease-of-setup of low-cost model
rubrics_metrics.description: The low per-article costs (Scholastica $10/submission plus modest DOI costs) are reproducible; setting up a journal with Scholastica (without DOIs/ISSN/custom website) can be done in about half an hour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Main work is assembling an editorial board, deciding policy, soliciting and publicizing the journal; administrative tasks like DOIs and ISSN require some backup but are manageable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author control over images and link maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: At launch the choice of images is controlled by Scholastica, but the editors plan to allow authors to have a say. Author homepage links are included and can be modified manually if authors change affiliation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan to permit changing images on existing articles and to update broken/out-of-date external links when notified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support for exploratory browsing beyond algorithmic suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial introductions and article images aim to restore a browsing experience where readers stumble across interesting papers that neither they nor recommendation algorithms would have surfaced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the site to enable serendipitous discovery akin to browsing print journals, not merely algorithmic 'related content' suggestions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical publishing workflow (post-acceptance)
rubrics_metrics.description: After acceptance, the author submits a revision to arXiv incorporating referees' comments; the journal ensures editorial introduction and metadata are prepared and then 'publishes' by linking to the arXiv version.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This workflow preserves the arXiv as the canonical host while allowing editorial enhancements and metadata curation by the journal.
